verses.text: The whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled themselves together at Shiloh, and set up the Tent of Meeting there. The land was subdued before them.
Seven tribes remained among the children of Israel, which had not yet divided their inheritance.
Joshua said to the children of Israel, “How long will you neglect to go in to possess the land, which Yahweh, the God of your fathers, has given you?
Appoint for yourselves three men from each tribe. I will send them, and they shall arise, walk through the land, and describe it according to their inheritance; and they shall come to me.
They shall divide it into seven portions. Judah shall live in his borders on the south, and the house of Joseph shall live in their borders on the north.
You shall survey the land into seven parts, and bring the description here to me; and I will cast lots for you here before Yahweh our God.

However, the Levites have no portion among you; for the priesthood of Yahweh is their inheritance. Gad, Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance east of the Jordan, which Moses the servant of Yahweh gave them.”
The men arose and went. Joshua commanded those who went to survey the land, saying, “Go walk through the land, survey it, and come again to me. I will cast lots for you here before Yahweh in Shiloh.”
The men went and passed through the land, and surveyed it by cities into seven portions in a book. They came to Joshua to the camp at Shiloh.
Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before Yahweh. There Joshua divided the land to the children of Israel according to their divisions.
The lot of the tribe of the children of Benjamin came up according to their families. The border of their lot went out between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph.
Their border on the north quarter was from the Jordan. The border went up to the side of Jericho on the north, and went up through the hill country westward. It ended at the wilderness of Beth Aven.
The border passed along from there to Luz, to the side of Luz (also called Bethel), southward. The border went down to Ataroth Addar, by the mountain that lies on the south of Beth Horon the lower.

The border extended, and turned around on the west quarter southward, from the mountain that lies before Beth Horon southward; and ended at Kiriath Baal (also called Kiriath Jearim), a city of the children of Judah. This was the west quarter.
The south quarter was from the farthest part of Kiriath Jearim. The border went out westward, and went out to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.

The border went down to the farthest part of the mountain that lies before the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is in the valley of Rephaim northward. It went down to the valley of Hinnom, to the side of the Jebusite southward, and went down to En Rogel.
It extended northward, went out at En Shemesh, and went out to Geliloth, which is over against the ascent of Adummim. It went down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.
It passed along to the side over against the Arabah northward, and went down to the Arabah.
The border passed along to the side of Beth Hoglah northward; and the border ended at the north bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan. This was the south border.
The Jordan was its border on the east quarter. This was the inheritance of the children of Benjamin, by the borders around it, according to their families.
Now the cities of the tribe of the children of Benjamin according to their families were Jericho, Beth Hoglah, Emek Keziz,
Beth Arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel,
Avvim, Parah, Ophrah,
Chephar Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba; twelve cities with their villages.
Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth,
Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah,
Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,
Zelah, Eleph, the Jebusite (also called Jerusalem), Gibeath, and Kiriath; fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the children of Benjamin according to their families.

footnotes.content: Shiloh becomes the gathering place, and the Tent of Meeting is pitched there—not in conquest's rush, but in deliberate worship. The land is subdued; now comes the patient work of dividing it rightly among God's people. This is how it looks when faith settles: we worship before we claim.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven tribes still wait for their inheritance. There's no hurry in the text, and no shame either—this is how the Lord orders the giving of His gifts. What we're given comes in His time, not ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua's words carry a gentle urgency: 'How long will you neglect?' He's not angry, but he knows that delay itself becomes a kind of sin—a refusal of what God has already offered. We, too, are called to claim our inheritance, not from greed, but from trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-one men are sent out—three from each of seven tribes—to walk the land and describe it. Notice: they go on foot, they see with their own eyes, they return with knowledge. This is how the Lord often works: He sends us into the world to learn Him, not to sit idle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven portions, and Judah's place is settled in the south, Joseph's house in the north. There's an order here, a architecture to how the Lord divides. Even in distribution, we see His hand arranging things with care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The surveyors are to bring their findings back, and Joshua will cast lots 'here before Yahweh.' This is faith at work: we do our homework, we gather what we know, and then we release the outcome to God's wisdom. The casting of lots was how Israel invited the Lord's direct hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Levites receive no land-portion; their inheritance is the priesthood itself and the Lord's service. What seems like less—no fields to till, no borders to defend—is actually the greater calling. Some are called to stand closer to the altar than others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men set out to survey, and Joshua repeats his charge: 'Go walk through the land, survey it, and come again.' There's something almost tender in this repetition—he's not harsh, but clear. He knows the work matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The surveyors return with a written record—descriptions divided into seven portions, all written down in a book. The Lord's people were people of order and record. They brought knowledge back to their leader, just as the Lord asks us to tend what He gives us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua casts the lots at Shiloh, 'before Yahweh,' and the divisions are finalized. The casting of lots invoked God's direct wisdom; it was not chance, but holy surrender. We, too, can trust that the Lord is present even in the decisions that feel uncertain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The lot falls to Benjamin, and his inheritance is marked: between Judah's sons and Joseph's sons, smaller but real. Sometimes our place seems crowded between greater powers, yet the Lord sees and names us fully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benjamin's northern border runs from the Jordan toward Jericho, up through hill country to Beth Aven's wilderness. These place-names mark real boundaries—borders that Benjamites would walk, know, defend, and call home. Our inheritance, too, has a shape and a place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Luz (Bethel) the border descends to Ataroth Addar, following the mountain south of Beth Horon. Each turn, each landmark, marks where one family's gift ends and another's begins. The Lord is a God of exact boundaries, of giving each what is truly theirs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The western border curves southward from Beth Horon to Kiriath Jearim. In these boundary-lines we see the Lord's care: each border is drawn, witnessed, made real. Our own life-boundaries—work, rest, family, calling—are no less carefully held by Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Kiriath Jearim westward to the spring of Nephtoah waters—the border follows the land itself, its shape and flow. The Lord doesn't impose arbitrary lines; He reads the earth as a book and divides it with wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Down to the mountain before Hinnom valley, to Rephaim, to the Jebusite's side, and to En Rogel—each name marks a place where enemies dwelt or battles would come. Benjamin's inheritance touches these contested lands. Sometimes God calls us to dwell near the border, where faith is most tested.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From En Shemesh northward through Geliloth, along Adummim's rise, to Bohan's stone—these markers are real men's names and real people's boundaries. The Lord works through particulars: through named things and named people, not abstractions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The border passes alongside the Arabah northward and down into it—following the natural contours of the dry land. There's a trust here: the Lord's borders follow reality, not wishful thinking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beth Hoglah marks the northern reach; the Salt Sea's bay marks the southern edge—and the Jordan itself runs the eastern border. Benjamin is bounded by water and by named places, making the inheritance real and defensible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The Jordan was its border on the east quarter'—a statement of finality and belonging. The tribes have their land; Benjamin has his boundary; each family knows where they stand. This is how the Lord makes us secure: with clear borders and a named place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jericho, Beth Hoglah, Emek Keziz—these cities are named. Jericho itself, once an enemy fortress, now belongs to Benjamin. The Lord gives us both land and cities; He transforms what was enemy territory into home. These place-names are reminders of that gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beth Arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel—each city represents not just walls and gates, but families, markets, wells, and the daily life of worship and work. When Scripture lists cities this way, it reminds us that the Lord cares about every place His people dwell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Avvim, Parah, Ophrah—three more cities in Benjamin's lot. Some we know well by name from Scripture; others are barely more than a word to us. Yet each one was home to families who loved, worked, struggled, and prayed. Every place matters to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chephar Ammoni, Ophni, and Geba make twelve—the first count of Benjamin's cities is complete. Twelve is the number of God's people, His tribes, His fullness. Even in the listing of cities, we see the Lord's pattern and purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth—more cities follow. Gibeon, especially, will loom large in later days: the place where the Gibeonites made their covenant with Joshua, where the sun stood still in battle. The Lord knows each place's future before it unfolds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah—three more names in the list. With each city named, Benjamin's inheritance grows more solid, more real. What seemed distant in promise becomes concrete in place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah—the list continues toward its end. These names were household words to Benjamites; to us they are echoes. Yet the Lord remembers each one, each stone, each family that dwelt there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zelah, Eleph, Jerusalem (the Jebusite city), Gibeath, and Kiriath—fourteen cities in this final count, rounding Benjamin's full inheritance. Jerusalem itself is named as the Jebusite hold; it will not become David's city for generations yet, but the Lord knew even then. He sees the future of every place He gives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
